claims.text: An optimal, moderate degree of chemical disorder enhances superconductivity by strengthening electron-phonon coupling.
Excessive chemical disorder increases electron scattering and degrades the superconducting critical temperature.
The starting material is a solid-solution alloy containing at least five elements, each at no less than 5 atomic percent.
The annealed starting material has moderate atomic ordering.
Rapid quenching increases chemical disorder relative to the annealed sample.
Overall composition, phase purity, and measurement conditions will be held constant while thermal processing is varied.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder influences the local electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes in the local density of states at the Fermi level alter the electron-scattering rate.
Chemical short-range order can modify the phonon density of states in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Moderate disorder can create beneficial local bonding variations that enhance electron-phonon coupling.
Very high disorder increases electron scattering, reduces Cooper-pair formation, and lowers Tc.
The rapidly quenched sample will have a lower Tc than the annealed baseline.
The rapidly quenched sample will have a broader superconducting transition than the annealed baseline.
The broader transition and lower Tc would reflect degraded pairing efficiency caused by excessive scattering.
The hypothesis is restricted to single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloys containing at least five elements at 5 atomic percent or more each.
The disorder threshold separating beneficial and detrimental behavior is undefined and may depend on alloy composition.
Tc can be compared using resistivity and magnetic-susceptibility measurements.
X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy can verify the intended difference in chemical disorder between the annealed and quenched samples.
Failure of the quenched sample to show a significant Tc reduction, or observation of a sharper transition, would falsify the hypothesis.
